dna: The 1970s splintered into diverse movements — disco united dancefloors, punk rejected excess, prog pushed technical limits, and funk made rhythm king. FM radio and vinyl culture fueled discovery.
Pop and disco favored verse-chorus with extended dance breaks. Prog epics spanned 10–20 minutes with multiple movements. Punk stripped songs to under three minutes of raw energy.
Moog synthesizer, clavinet, wah-wah guitar, Rhodes piano, string sections, slap bass, TR-77 drum machine, and the iconic talkbox.
Disco thrived on major-key progressions with lush extensions (7ths, 9ths). Punk used power chords (I–IV–V). Prog explored odd meters and complex modulations. Funk centered on one-chord vamps.

dna: The 1980s married technology and pop — MTV made music visual, digital synths replaced analog, drum machines became standard, and CD replaced vinyl. Excess and ambition defined the era.
Verse-chorus-bridge ruled pop. Tracks averaged 3:30–4:30 with prominent intros and instrumental breaks. Power ballads featured slow builds to soaring climaxes.
Yamaha DX7, Roland Juno-106, LinnDrum, TR-808, gated reverb snare, keytar, slap bass, Floyd Rose tremolo guitar, and the Fairlight CMI sampler.
Major-key anthems dominated (I–V–vi–IV). New wave favored minor keys with angular arpeggios. Hair metal mixed pentatonic riffs with power ballad chord progressions.

dna: The 90s birthed alternative culture — grunge rejected 80s excess, hip-hop hit its golden age, electronic music invaded clubs, and the internet began reshaping music distribution forever.
Grunge used quiet-loud dynamics (verse-chorus-verse). Hip-hop evolved from boom-bap to complex flows. Pop and R&B embraced elaborate bridges and key changes.
Distortion pedals, drop-D tuning, MPC sampler, Roland TR-909, turntables, Auto-Tune (late 90s), wah pedals, and the Fender Jaguar/Jazzmaster.
Grunge favored power chords in minor keys. Britpop embraced major-key anthems. Hip-hop sampled jazz and soul. R&B used extended chords (7ths, 9ths, 11ths) over slow grooves.

dna: The 2000s saw music go digital — Napster disrupted distribution, iPod changed listening, MySpace launched careers, and genres splintered into countless micro-scenes online.
Nu-metal mixed rap verses with screamed choruses. Emo used quiet-loud dynamics with confessional bridges. Pop embraced Auto-Tune. Indie rock returned to stripped-down verse-chorus.
7-string guitars, Pro Tools, Auto-Tune, MPC 2000, Roland V-Drums, turntables, drop-B tuning, and the rise of laptop production with Ableton and Logic.
Nu-metal used drop-tuned power chords and chromatic riffs. Emo favored expressive minor keys with octave melodies. Crunk relied on simple synth hooks. Indie rock embraced angular progressions.

dna: Streaming reshaped everything — Spotify playlists became gatekeepers, SoundCloud launched careers, K-pop went global, and the album gave way to singles and playlist-friendly tracks.
Pop embraced the hook-first approach — chorus within 30 seconds. Trap favored looping structures. EDM built around drop-build-drop. Lo-fi used ambient, repetitive forms.
TR-808, Serum synth, Auto-Tune, Ableton Live, lo-fi tape emulation, sidechain compression, vocal chops, and pitch-shifted 808 bass slides.
Trap uses dark minor keys with simple melodies. EDM favors emotional progressions (vi–IV–I–V). K-pop blends Western pop harmony with unexpected modulations. Lo-fi leans on jazzy 7th and 9th chords.

dna: Ad music must embody the brand's personality in sound. Luxury brands need elegance, tech brands need innovation, lifestyle brands need warmth — every note serves the identity.
Commercials run to exact seconds — 15, 30, or 60. Music must hit emotional beats, support dialogue windows, and land a clean ending at the exact cutoff.
Music drives 60% of a commercial's emotional impact. The right soundtrack makes audiences feel trust, excitement, or nostalgia — the emotions that drive purchase decisions.
Sonic branding creates memory hooks. A catchy jingle or distinctive sound logo makes the brand stick in the listener's mind long after the ad ends.

dna: Background music exists to enhance an environment without demanding attention. It supports mood, fills silence, and adds emotional texture to physical or digital spaces.
Low dynamic contrast is key — no sudden peaks or drops. Consistent volume and energy keep the music unobtrusive while maintaining a steady emotional tone throughout.
Acoustic guitar, soft piano, ambient pads, light strings, and gentle percussion. Instruments are chosen for warmth and smoothness over edge or complexity.
Simple, resolved chord progressions in major or mixolydian modes. Avoid tension-heavy dissonance — the goal is comfort, not surprise.

dna: Corporate music must feel polished and trustworthy. No rough edges, no extreme emotions — the sound conveys competence, confidence, and credibility.
Business audiences span all demographics. The music stays broadly appealing — modern but not trendy, emotional but not divisive, energetic but not aggressive.
Presentations have variable lengths. Corporate music needs clean cut points, extendable loops, and energy shifts that editors can align with slides and segments.
Most corporate content features narration or live speaking. Music stays clear of vocal frequencies, with low enough volume to support rather than compete.

dna: Film music serves the story. Every cue aligns with plot beats — foreshadowing with subtle motifs, underscoring emotion, and punctuating dramatic turning points.
A single film score may span tenderness, terror, triumph, and tragedy. The music must shift seamlessly across the full emotional spectrum.
Strings, brass, woodwinds, percussion, and choir form the backbone. Modern film scoring adds electronic textures and hybrid elements for contemporary impact.
Film music lives alongside dialogue, Foley, and sound effects. Frequency awareness and dynamic restraint ensure the score enhances without competing.

dna: Game music must respond to player state — intensity rising in combat, easing during exploration, and signaling transitions between gameplay phases.
Most game tracks loop seamlessly. Clean loop points with smooth transitions ensure the music never feels repetitive during extended play sessions.
A single game may need orchestral boss themes, ambient cave music, chiptune minigames, and electronic menu screens — all cohesive within one soundtrack.
Victory fanfares, defeat stings, discovery jingles, and tension drones create instant emotional feedback that reinforces gameplay mechanics.
